summaries.example: Imagine two students solve the same puzzle in different ways. Both answers are correct, but one method may make the reason clearer, use fewer tools, or be easier for others to check. Philosophers of mathematical practice ask similar questions about proofs and other mathematical work.
summaries.summary: The philosophy of mathematical practice, often shortened to PMP, asks philosophical questions by looking closely at real mathematical activity. Instead of treating mathematics only as a finished collection of true statements, it studies how mathematicians explore ideas, write proofs, use symbols and pictures, work with one another, and use computers. PMP can examine every area of mathematics, from geometry and arithmetic to topology, algebra, analysis, and set theory. It also pays attention to the history of mathematics and to the people doing mathematics. Some philosophers study the final products, such as proofs and theories. Others study the process: the choices, habits, tools, and communities that produce them. The source describes several valuable features of mathematical work. Rigor helps make results reliable. Explanation helps show why a result is true. Purity asks whether a proof uses methods belonging to the problem or subject. Visualization can make relationships easier to see. These features may support one another, but they can also pull in different directions. For example, a very strict method may sometimes make progress harder, while a diagram may help with understanding even though it is not written as a formal proof. PMP uses case studies and historical examples rather than relying only on very general principles. It does not have one single method or one complete definition. Some researchers see it as a partner to traditional work on foundations; others see it as a stronger alternative. The main lesson is that understanding mathematics requires looking at both its finished results and the human activities that create and assess them.
key_ideas: Mathematics is more than a finished list of answers. It also includes the activities people use to discover, explain, and check results.
This approach studies many areas of mathematics, not only numbers, logic, and sets.
History, human thinking, teamwork, notation, diagrams, and computers can all help us understand mathematical work.
A proof can be correct but still leave people wondering why the result is true. Other proofs may explain the reason better.
There is more than one view about whether this approach should add to traditional foundations or challenge them.
summaries.why_it_matters: This approach reminds us that mathematics is a living human activity. It helps explain why people value clear proofs, helpful pictures, good questions, useful definitions, and reliable tools—not just correct answers. It also shows why new technologies and teamwork can raise fresh questions about what it means to understand and know mathematics.

important_terms.definition: The study of philosophical questions that grow out of the ways mathematicians actually work.
A carefully reasoned argument that supports a mathematical result.
A quality that makes mathematical work useful for learning or checking, such as clarity or explanatory power.
Using pictures, diagrams, or spatial arrangements to help think about mathematics.

questions_to_think_about: Why might mathematicians prove the same result in more than one way?
Can a picture help someone understand a proof without being the whole proof?
Should a computer-assisted proof count as a proof if people cannot check every tiny step by hand?

summaries.example: Consider a theorem about integers that was first proved with advanced tools from another area of mathematics and later proved using only elementary number theory. The later proof may be valued for its purity: it stays within the conceptual territory suggested by the theorem. Yet the original proof might still be shorter or useful in another way. This illustrates why correctness is not the only feature mathematicians assess.
summaries.summary: The philosophy of mathematical practice (PMP) is a broad, practice-oriented cluster of approaches in the philosophy of mathematics. Its common commitment is to investigate philosophical problems through the inner workings of mathematics as it is actually performed, historically and today. This shifts attention away from a picture of mathematics as a static body of propositions represented by formal theories. PMP asks what mathematicians do, which mathematical domains they work in, what kinds of agents and communities they form, and what methods and tools shape their activity. The approach therefore includes geometry, arithmetic, algebra, analysis, topology, set theory, category theory, and other fields, rather than treating a small foundational core as representative of mathematics as a whole. It also studies notation, visualization, explanation, proof development, collaboration, testimony, disagreement, cognition, and computational technology. Methodologically, much PMP is bottom-up: detailed case studies inform philosophical analysis. It also often combines descriptive and normative concerns. A purely descriptive account records practices, while a normative account asks which standards should govern mathematical justification; many practice-based investigations connect the two by examining norms as they function in real mathematical communities. The notion of practice itself spans a product/process spectrum. Some studies focus on products such as proofs, definitions, diagrams, and theories; others emphasize agents, communities, research programs, and the processes through which products arise. key_ideas: PMP broadens the subject matter of philosophy of mathematics from foundational questions about arithmetic, logic, and sets to practices across mathematical fields.
It treats mathematicians as historically situated agents whose cognitive, social, and technological circumstances can affect mathematical development.
Its methods often occupy a spectrum between descriptive accounts of what mathematicians do and normative accounts of what they ought to do.
The term practice has a product/process ambiguity: research may focus on proofs and theories, on mathematical activity, or on positions between these extremes.
Epistemic virtues—including purity, explanation, rigor, and visualizability—show why mathematical evaluation involves more than truth and formal correctness.
PMP contains both ecumenical views, which complement foundational work, and anti-foundational views, which oppose foundationalist priorities.
summaries.why_it_matters: PMP matters because it expands what counts as philosophically significant mathematical evidence. It can illuminate features that a purely foundational picture tends to leave aside: how proofs persuade and explain, how diagrams guide inference, how communities distribute knowledge, and how computers alter standards of verification. It also encourages a more careful view of disagreement. Practice-based approaches do not yield one unanimous doctrine; they include complementary and oppositional positions concerning foundations, formalization, and the proper aims of philosophy of mathematics.

important_terms.definition: A broad family of approaches that investigates philosophical questions arising from actual, historical, and contemporary mathematical activity.
A program seeking basic principles or structures on which mathematics can be grounded, often emphasizing logic, arithmetic, set theory, or formal systems.
A method that begins with detailed mathematical cases and develops philosophical conclusions from them, rather than applying a general theory first.
A feature of a proof valued when it avoids concepts considered foreign to the problem, theorem, or mathematical discipline involved.
A feature of a proof or theory that helps show why a result holds, not merely that it follows.
The property of establishing a conclusion through acceptable deductive steps; its standards can change with mathematical practices and tools.
The ability of diagrams or other representations to make mathematical relations cognitively accessible and support reasoning.
A software system that assists in constructing or checking formal mathematical proofs.

questions_to_think_about: If an informal proof could in principle be translated into a formal derivation, does that capture everything the proof does for mathematicians?
Can a diagram contribute to rigorous reasoning, or must rigor ultimately be independent of visual representation?
When a proof is shorter but less explanatory, and another is longer but more illuminating, which should be preferred?
How might computer-assisted proofs and interactive theorem provers change standards of trust, understanding, or rigor?
Does studying actual practice provide local answers to philosophical problems that general theories cannot settle?

summaries.example: Suppose your class must show that a certain pattern always works. One student writes a short chain of symbols. Another draws a picture that reveals the pattern. A third explains why the pattern works in every case. All three may help, but they do different jobs. Philosophers of mathematical practice study these differences instead of asking only whether the final answer is true.
summaries.summary: The philosophy of mathematical practice (PMP) studies philosophical questions by examining mathematics as mathematicians actually do it. This includes informal exploration, conjecture, proof, explanation, use of notation and diagrams, collaboration, historical change, and interaction with computers. It differs from approaches that focus mainly on mathematics as a fixed collection of formal theories or on the problem of how humans gain access to abstract mathematical objects. PMP does not reject those questions in every case, but it argues that they do not exhaust the philosophy of mathematics. It widens the range of mathematical areas under study, including geometry, algebra, analysis, topology, category theory, and set theory. It also widens the range of mathematical subjects: not idealized thinkers alone, but historically situated people and communities with ordinary cognitive limits, shared practices, and dependence on one another. This makes social and cognitive questions relevant. For example, mathematicians may accept results proved by others, use testimony, debate standards, or rely on tools to check difficult arguments. PMP commonly favors a bottom-up method. Instead of beginning with a universal theory of proof or explanation, philosophers may investigate particular examples and ask what those examples reveal. The method can be descriptive, normative, or a mixture: it can describe how mathematicians work, assess the standards they use, or explain how those standards are connected. The source also distinguishes two meanings of practice. A product-oriented study examines proofs, definitions, diagrams, and theories. A process-oriented study examines the agents, communities, activities, and historical settings that produce them. Much work lies between the two. PMP:
key_ideas: Traditional philosophy of mathematics often concentrated on foundations, abstract objects, and very general questions. PMP asks what may be learned by studying actual mathematical practices.
PMP treats mathematics as varied rather than monolithic. Different subjects, tools, histories, and communities can matter.
Researchers disagree about whether PMP complements foundational projects or should replace their priorities.
Mathematical proofs and theories can be judged by virtues such as correctness, explanatory power, purity, rigor, simplicity, and visualizability.
The approach uses historical and contemporary case studies, and it may draw on psychology, sociology, education, linguistics, and other fields.
A mathematical practice can mean the products of activity, the activity itself, or a position somewhere between those two meanings.
summaries.why_it_matters: Studying mathematical practice helps explain why mathematicians care about more than obtaining correct conclusions. They also seek methods that are illuminating, economical, transferable, appropriately rigorous, or visually helpful. This perspective can make mathematics seem less like a finished machine and more like an evolving discipline shaped by reasoning, communication, history, and technology. It also gives philosophers better tools for discussing what mathematical understanding and knowledge involve.

important_terms.definition: A field of philosophy that studies questions arising from real mathematical work, including proving, explaining, representing, collaborating, and using tools.
The view that mathematics should be understood partly through its development over time and the practices of mathematicians.
A general system of basic assumptions, rules, or structures intended to support mathematical reasoning.
An approach that starts with particular mathematical examples or episodes and uses them to develop broader philosophical ideas.
A desirable feature of mathematical work that helps it produce, communicate, or support knowledge.
A proof feature involving the use of methods that stay within the relevant mathematical subject or the concepts in the statement.
An account that helps us understand why a mathematical fact holds, rather than merely confirming that it holds.
The standard that a proof's conclusion follows through acceptable reasoning; philosophers debate how informal proofs meet this standard.

questions_to_think_about: Why might a mathematician want several proofs of the same theorem?
Can a proof be rigorous and still fail to explain the result well?
When does using a method from another area of mathematics improve a proof, and when might it make the proof less satisfying?
Should mathematics be studied mainly as a system of truths, as a human activity, or as both?
What new philosophical questions arise when computers help create or check proofs?
